Follow up: If I am seeing the "Sorry...try again in a little while" message, is everyone seeing that, or are there a maximum number of people currnelty in the site, and I am just queued?
ELI5: What happens to the servers when a bunch of people all go to a site at once, and how do they fix it?

I assume that before the Reddit exodus to Voat, Atko didn't expect that so many people would come here at such a fast rate. As he mentioned in one of his posts, he intended Voat to be a place for his family and friends to connect with each other, not for the mainstream Internet user to post anything they liked.

The Voat servers weren't ready to take in a large haul of requests from multiple users around the world, therefore causing the webpages to run really slowly or not at all due to 'bottlenecks' (not enough pathways technically for data to be passed to and from Voat's web server at once) as not enough bandwidth had been allocated. To fix this, Atko will need to upgrade Voat's web server to be more powerful so running at a faster speed (e.g 1000 Mbps) so that thousands or tens of thousands of requests can be made in a single time without crashing the web server due to a large volume that the server cannot handle. I don't really know of Voat's network configuration but this seems most applicable in this sense.

Directed at your other question, there must be a queue because sometimes I am able to load the front page or whichever subverse I am trying to access and sometimes I cannot. The Voat web server/s probably have a maximum capacity that it can hold before it just can't take it anymore. Thus, when the server is at its maximum, it displays a message as you mentioned above. In order to fix this, the servers will need more broadband so that more users can make requests (load webpages by clicking links anywhere on any of the pages) concurrently with little delay.

You will have to be patient at this time until Atko and his team upgrade their servers and network infrastructure to be able to handle even more concurrent users at one time without bottlenecks so that users can make requests without being delayed or consistently receiving errors.

The answer to your question is both simple and complicated.

In this case, voat likely only had a couple of servers and there is a finite number of concurrent users those servers can handle. When the maelstrom of reddit users suddenly started coming here the servers were quickly inundated and that led to resources being overwhelmed and the worst case scenario to happen: the systems just didn't respond. The only way to fix this is to add capacity to whatever is the choke point, be it the network, server capacity (RAM, CPU, etc), or (again, most likely in this scenario) the number of servers that handle the web requests.

The best analogy is to think of it like a highway entrance ramp. On a normal day the ramp is used by a subdivision of 100 houses. The ramp was designed with those 100 homes in mind. Now imagine if a whole new subdivision with 1000 homes was built overnight. The morning commute the next day would suck because the ramp didn't have the capacity for a 10x increase in traffic.

To continue with the on ramp analogy, the reason the ramp was designed for only 100 houses is because on ramps aren't cheap. They are expensive to build and there are not-insignificant costs to maintain them. Servers are the same.

This is one of the most challenging things about architecting new systems. You have to balance the cost. The admins don't want 'Atlanta freeways at 5pm' but they also don't want to pay for 'the bridge to nowhere'. I'm sure if someone told the admins a week ago this was coming they would have been better prepared.

As for your follow up, that is the complicated part. There are a bunch of both low and high tech ways of giving a 'server busy' message. Many work off a timer. So if a request has been in one state for X seconds (there are dozens, maybe thousands, of states on a request such as checking if the user us logged in, if they have the night time theme loaded, etc), the server recognizes the thread is hung and kills it. Under normal circumstances this would imply something went bad with the request and it hung so it's best to just kill the request and release the resources it has allocated.

More high tech ways of resource monitoring actively look at disk i/o, CPU load etc. and will also start killing threads when needed.

It's always best to hand a user something, even if it's an timeout page, than to hand back nothing. So no, when you see those messages the servers has basically said 'sorry, come back later' and forgot about you.

I've also seen a lot the the attention Voat is getting focus around the idea that it's now the place all of the worst/shittiest people from reddit will end up, and in my brief time here, I've seen that concern/opinion floating around the voat community as well.

I did not participate in the fph subreddit, or honestly even care about it one way or the other, and I can say that about probably hundreds or thousands of other subs. There is one major thing that applies to any forum or otherwise user-generated-content-site: there are probably going to be things that would elicit reactions from meh/not-my-cup-of-tea to holy shit, that is gross and/or really offensive. The beauty about these types of sites the internet in general is that no one forces to you go there or view said content or uncomfortable opinions. For example, I really enjoy /r/linux, but avoid /r/spacedicks like the plague. Pretty simple!

Regarding the situation on reddit over the past few days, media outlets, blogs, and naive redditors can focus on whatever aspect of it that they want, but in my opinion, despite what reddit hq is spouting, morals and 'wanting to create a safe space' could not have less to do with what we are seeing. They want to continue to monetize and drive the site into more of curated (by corporations) model. Having popular subreddits constantly on the front page that display possibly offensive opinions and material is counterproductive to that end, and it's as simple as that. That's why we see incredibly racist or homophobic small subreddits remaining active. The 'we prohibit certain actions, not opinions' is BS. They are trying to save-face with advertisers and other corporate interests.

Anyway, /rant. I'm not here for the purpose of shitting on fat people, but rather because the recent events on reddit were the last straw, for me, in a trend that I was seeing. I want to participate in free, open, honest conversations and communities online. What that means for the community in general does include possibly offensive or otherwise uncomfortable topics, groups, interactions, etc. ,but you have to take the good with the bad if you really want truly free speech. The good news is, you can totally avoid the shit you don't like!

Anyway, Voat admins and those in charge: please keep this community and site free and free from censorship via corporate interests and people will willingly donate! I already did, twice!
